title: Mountains, Waters and Sesshin, Part 3
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett continues the history of Samish sesshin into the 2000s, tracing how Richard Baker's fall at San Francisco Zen Center sent former students back to practice with Norman Fischer, then turns to sections seven through ten of Dogen's Mountains and Waters Sutra. Along the way Nomon describes an orthodox rabbi who prayed by the gazebo during morning service and the 2008 mini practice period, when Norman opened each talk by appreciating the previous evening's. Dogen's passage on water, which dragons see as a palace and hungry ghosts see as pus and blood, leads Nomon to community as the place where people are left alone to work through their stuff. Nomon closes with John Wiley's remark that he noticed how beautiful it is here.

So, back a little bit to the history of Samish sesshin.
If you're just joining today, online or in there, maybe you'll later listen to the first two talks.
It took me two talks to get through the 1990s.
Now we're into the 2000s.
To fully understand what started happening here in sesshin in the 2000s, we actually have to go back to the early 1980s in San Francisco, oddly enough.
Our founding teacher Norman Fischer started practice in Berkeley in 1970 when he was 26.
It was actually just a little before Suzuki Roshi died.
He never met Suzuki Roshi, although he had a few opportunities to do so.
He didn't quite get around to it.
But he right away had a strong connection with the teacher in Berkeley, Sojun Mel Weitsman, who really kind of took him under his wing.
Norman found a spiritual home and a practice that helped him start to become a little more grounded.
Mel quietly supported this smart and, by all accounts of people I've talked to, pretty erratic and goofy young guy.
Norman was one of the first residents at Berkeley's Zen center, maybe even before they called it that.
It was Mel's house.
Mel really.
And then in 1976, by then married to his wife Kathy, and this year they celebrate their 50th anniversary, with two sons, soon to fall, like in the oven, they went off to Tassajara Monastery.
Can you imagine?
"Oh, we're having twins.
Let's go to a monastery."
But it made sense at the time.
And there Norman would spend the next years studying with Richard Baker.
Dick.
Norman always called him that to my hearing.
I never heard Norman say Baker Roshi.
Dick Baker, that's his name.
And Baker was by all accounts a brilliant leader and teacher.
And Norman actually was his jisha for a number of years, I think a little bit at Tassajara and then also when they moved to Green Gulch Farm in 1981.
Green Gulch had been operating for eight years at that point.
And Norman would go on to serve in pretty much all of the different leadership positions at Green Gulch.
He was the director there when I met him five years later, in 1986.
Eventually he was one of the abbots of the whole three-center establishment of San Francisco Zen Center, from 95 to 2000.
One can give many talks about the heady early days on the three campuses of San Francisco Zen Center.
It was an exciting and intense time.
But the karmic factor that affected us here so many years later, that I want to talk about, was Richard Baker Roshi's blowout in the early 80s.
And the way I remember Norman telling it is this.
Dick worked really, really hard for the community.
He got a lot done.
He was very good at whatever he set his mind to.
If you read more about the details or history you'll see it.
And so it just seemed natural to him that he needed a lot of support to keep doing what he was doing.
Doing more and more needed a lot of support.
Very logical.

So he needed a nice car, a comfortable car, and a Zen student to drive him back and forth between the three centers, a couple of hours driving here and there pretty frequently, because he was the teacher at all three centers.
So he was in motion.
So sure, the community bought him a nice BMW.
He needed, I don't know why this sticks in my head, but he needed duplicate libraries.
All the same books, shelved in the same order, so he could quickly just grab the book he was thinking of when he was writing the Dharma talk.
He probably didn't have much time to prepare it.
And he was not just the head teacher, more or less the only teacher for a few hundred students.
He was absolutely the head of the whole organization, running things from stem to stern.
It wasn't a board of directors, but they pretty much just supported whatever he wanted to do.
And it wasn't just the significant Zen center, the largest Zen center in the West in fact, with three residential places.
They were also running several businesses.
They had a bakery, a meditation cushion sewing business.
They had a restaurant, which would go on to get lots of Michelin stars and stuff.
And he was running it all.
He was also an incredible fundraiser, constantly talking to people with resources, and they would write large checks.
Very charming, too, by all accounts.
People wanted to hang out with this guy.
So now all of that at the same time, and you wonder if maybe he was a little bipolar or something.
So anyway, Dick Baker was given the title Roshi by his students, because they were used to that with Suzuki Roshi.
And he was his sole heir before he died.
He really just needed everything arranged so it would work.
Apparently he also needed some demonstrations of everyone's respect for this arrangement.

I remember they told me at Green Gulch when I was first there that whenever he was driving away from the valley of Green Gulch up towards San Francisco, probably, they would all go line up on the driveway and bow to his BMW as it drove by.
There's a bit of formality traditionally when an abbot comes or goes from the monastery, so he wasn't totally making this up.
Still.
And so eventually, and this is how Norman told it, as I remember anyway, Richard Baker also felt like he needed several girlfriends.
And it turns out at least one of them was married.
But in a way that doesn't matter.
You just think for half a second about the insane power imbalance in that situation and the utter inappropriateness of them having any relationships like that at all.
Consent is dubious.
So I think now, in retrospect, we're like, "Oh yeah, it all made sense to them at the time, what was going on."
They were working really, really hard.
They really believed in what they were doing.
They were not just serious about Zen because it's cool and it helps us and it helps the world, which is maybe what we might say.
But having some other things in your life, maybe, that was it.
Living in the Zen Center was their entire life.
And they were actually creating a whole tradition, modern, integrated, integrated and just wise, enlightened.
They were constantly a perfect society that really would save the world.
A powerful alternative to the materialistic mainstream culture, which is an obvious thing to reject, right?
But I think now also they saw it as a powerful alternative to the ungrounded alternative hippie culture that many of them had come through and seen things fall apart.
This was right when most of the 1960s and 70s communes were happening and dissolved.
So what they were doing was a very big deal.
And I'm sure sometimes somebody would question this or that, but the basic premise, I think, was essentially just true.
So I think it's hard to imagine the sound of that bubble breaking and the pain of that bubble breaking when the news came out about Dick Baker's transgressions.
And most of them were kind of on the young side, too, from our perspective now.
Many still in their 20s and 30s.
And for some of them, this was their whole adult life.
Just after college or dropping out of college or not going to college, hearing there was this Zen master in California, you're going to stick out your thumb, right?
So then in fairly short order, as these things go, this incredible thing that had come together so powerfully fractured.
Roughly a third of the people kept their focus on Richard Baker's skills as a teacher, as their teacher.
I don't know if they were all apologists for his behavior, but that's where they kept their focus.
Some were, I think, apologists for his behavior.
It was a big deal.
But as a teacher, we're definitely considerable.
I've heard many stories about how insightful he was, how he would tell you just the one thing that you needed to hear.
Maybe you didn't want to hear it, but he was so [unclear: "changeable"].
Very intuitive, I think.
And so anyway, about a third of this group of, I don't know how many hundred, two or three hundred, something like that, went with him.
Started new communities in Colorado, a new community in Germany, [unclear: "welled up"].
I don't know if the third is the right number, but some number went with him.
Another third or so, this probably was a larger group, I'm not sure, another third or so stayed put.
This is our home.
They went through the hard, depressing slog of rebuilding and reinventing.
It was a really hard time, I think.
I remember somebody telling me that for several months after Baker was encouraged strongly to resign and leave, the Green Gulch Zendo was empty.
You've got to remember, that would never have been the case. [unclear: "Every month, it was exhausted"], and the Zendo was full.
So the schedule and the practice fell apart.
I'm sure people just felt terrible.
They couldn't keep doing it anymore.
About a third left formal practice altogether.
And that's what I'm getting to.
This is the group of interest to us.
Most of them had no savings, precious little work experience, and no real plan.
Things were, I think, relatively a little easier economically back then, especially for middle-class white folks.
The San Francisco Bay Area was a reasonable, affordable place to live, but not now, if you've been there in recent decades.
The 1980s economy was reasonably healthy.
So they could find their way.
Not easy, necessarily, but they had to work hard for a while.
Like, for example, Reza's teacher, Chris Fortin, and her husband, Bruce, are a good example.
They'd been at Green Gulch since pretty soon after the founding of it.
They went off about an hour and a half or so north of Green Gulch and found some rural property, a piece of land.
And then they paired up with another pair of fleeing Zennies to team up and pitch in, and somehow barely scraped enough together to buy the land and build a house themselves.
Bruce got a job at a retirement community as an administrator, eventually became the director.
Chris went back to school to become a psychotherapist.
I'm sure there were various odd jobs in there I don't know about.
Make it all work, get groceries.
They raised a child and lived their lives away from all that madness at the Zen Center.
I'm sure they sat together at home, but no going, no sangha.
No, no, no sangha, thank you.

And then Norman, who was ready to leave the establishment because he was one of the stayers, one of the muddled-throughers, which it seems like he did with pretty good cheer for some reason and a kind of balanced attitude.
You know, that Dick had done some bad stuff, you would never apologize for him, but that it was workable.
And then here was this practice and this place of practice.
"Let's roll up our sleeves, folks."
But then he was done.
He'd done enough time by 2000, and he left the Zen Center and started his own organization, as you probably know, called Everyday Zen.
That was his focus: practice in everyday life.
You don't need to live in a big center.
And I guess there was enough of a Zen Center telegraph functioning that the word got out.
Of course, by then there was the Internet, too.
I created Everyday Zen's first website.
It was early in the days of the website.
So they remembered this guy, Norman.
He was their friend, their colleague, their peer.
And here he was teaching outside of all that, where they had these complicated memories.
So many of them thought to themselves, Let's go see what Norman's up to.
Enough time had gone by, right?
Fifteen years.
And so they did.
Norman and his Everyday Zen attracted a good number of those people who had left after the disaster and had been his peers back in the day.
One nexus here is that Richard Baker had done a very large priest ordination in 1980.
I've seen a picture of the Buddha Hall at San Francisco Zen Center.
There was no room for anyone but the ordinees.
It was filled with space.
I think at least 30 people ordained at one big ceremony.
Having done this ceremony, I cannot imagine.
Although I'm sure Baker had a lot of assistants helping him prepare all this stuff.
I'm sure he did.
Several of these same people who came to practice with Norman later at Everyday Zen were ordained with him in that big ceremony.
Kathy was ordained at the same time, with his wife.
But they hadn't continued formal training, right?
They'd been living in the woods, like Bruce and Chris, having a regular life.
But the practice had never left their hearts.
How would it?

While Norman was doing all the formal steps, like being shuso, head student, and learning about priestcraft and studying and getting to know lots of dharma classes and teach lots of dharma classes and receive dharma transmission, they'd been learning about the world.
So they were peers in one way, but in another way Norman was now able to be their teacher.
And the way he's wired, that somehow worked.
It's easy to imagine that not working, isn't it?
Can you imagine yourself in that situation?
Yeah, I'm sure.
There's not always harmony in the Zen Center.
Probably many of them can remember some schmucky thing Norman had done at some point, right?
Because we all have that.
Apparently he wasn't always so careful about people's feelings.
And so they studied with him, and he started to do those formal steps and re-entered the practice.
But in this new way, not in the big center, but coming to Norman's place, going home again, this practice he called Everyday Zen.
Some had already ordained and he helped them along, some hadn't quite ordained and he ordained.
Some years later he transmitted them, helped them finish the training.
But here's the thing, though.
He wanted to study intensively with Norman in the 2000s, and there were not a lot of opportunities.
He kept Everyday Zen really simple after his experiences.
Weekly evening, one day sitting monthly or so, one sesshin a year is enough trouble.
But then his eager young students here and there put on their own sesshins, and Norman would go teach there.
So one of the main places you'd want to go if you were one of those people and wanted to study intensively with Norman was here.
Come here.
And it's not like we were exactly overrun by priests doing this kind of catch-up thing, but there was always a pretty good cadre of them.
Maybe they had a little outsized influence versus the number of human beings up there.
And people who weren't ordained, too.
People who just appreciated Norman from back in the day or increasingly in the present day.
So every year through the 2000s and the early 2010s, a good-sized contingent would fly up for sesshin.
Maybe five or six from the Bay Area, a few from New York, a few from Boston, one guy from Colorado every year.
Some years there were enough people that we would rent a shuttle bus to get them from Sea-Tac.
It's not so easy to get here.
And this year, Bobby was [unclear: "keeping this person alive out from Boston"].
And Jericho Samuel was following the footsteps of giants, hopping on a plane.
Also, starting in 2000, we started having Northwest native priests, too.
I was ordained in the year 2000, Kate and Michael in 2003, Rick Spencer in 2004.
We were a bit of a foursome from then, me, Kate and Michael, and Rick, until our dharma transmission in 2011.
And so the character of Samish sesshin really changed as a result of all this.
It was still sesshin.
The routine was always the same: zazen, service, silence, schedule.
But now it was suddenly also a kind of annual training monastery for novice priests and senior students and lay teachers.
All kinds of people who appreciated Norman wanted to be able to express their Dharma more than just sitting there looking at the wall.
So we started populating the positions with lots of people.
Different doshi every day.
People could practice.
And more than just that, Norman starts getting involved in all kinds of other Dharma projects.
And once he's unleashed, he's all over the place, traveling a lot.
He started doing retreats on Jewish meditation, mediation, and the law, with meditation, mindfulness in the corporate world, he's hanging out at Google, all kinds of things.
And so people from those worlds start coming too.
We had several rabbis, university professors, lawyers, all with some meditation experience.
It wasn't like we were just groupies.
They were meditators.
But many of them had never sat in sesshin before.
So we sometimes took a little energy to help them see what was going on here.
But they'd all study with Norman, and they all loved Norman, and so we therefore loved each other.
I remember one orthodox rabbi, I don't know if anyone remembers his name.
He felt it wasn't appropriate for him to do a Buddhist service.
He said everything else is fine.

So when we walked by on our way to the meal, we'd walk by him, gazing out towards the water with his yarmulke, doing his, what's it called, shucking?
Shuckling?
As he prayed and peeped quietly.

And he was generous there, often seeing people for as long as an hour.

A little bit later.
